items.title: Shuttle
items.text:
The script file package manager

Shuttle is an easy way to create, manage, and organize large and complex shell scripts.

items.title: FAQ
items.text:
What shells does shuttle support?

Shuttle supports sh, bash, and (partially) zsh scripts. By default, shuttle will install projects as bash scripts. Shuttle was designed for bash though, so bash is it's primary workspace. Shuttle was written in bash.

I installed a project, but I can't run it!

Shuttle installs projects to $HOME/.local/bin/ if you're running as a user, and /usr/local/bin/ if you're running as root. Ensure that those directories are inside your path.

How do I do that? Whats my shell's profile?

~/.bash_profile for bash ~/.zprofile for zsh

Add the following to your shell's profile:

export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/.local/bin"
export PATH="$PATH:/usr/local/bin"

Then restart your session. (logout, then login)

items.title: Developing with Shuttle
items.text:
Hello fellow scripter! You've officially reached the Shuttle Script Developer Documentation!

New? Looking to start? Follow our new developer guide. Veteran? Looking for new features? Check the changelog.

items.title: Master Tutorial
items.text:
Welcome to the master tutorial! In this guide you'll learn how to:

  • Make shuttle projects
  • Source project files
  • Learn special project folders

Thank you for choosing shuttle to organize and manage your projects!

items.title: Important notices
items.text:
This guide assumes you have basic familiarity with bash scripting. If you don't, consult the internet for a guide. This is not a "learn shell" guide.

This guide assumes you already have shuttle installed. If you don't, see installing.

Next step? Click "Creating a project" in the bottom-right corner!

items.title: Creating the project
items.text:
You'll start your learning by making a directory to store your shuttle project. Generally, projects are stored inside the ~/projects directory, but can be anywhere on your file system.

Luckily, shuttle makes project creation incredibly easy. There are two entire commands dedicated to it! In this guide, we'll create a project using the new command inside shuttle.

Remember! Shuttle comes with a built-in help command!

Use shuttle help <command> for an easy refrence to what the command does as well as what arguments it takes.

Create a new project using shuttle called 'project'
shuttle new project

Replace 'project' with the name you're calling your project. We'll be assuming the name of the project is project for the rest of this guide. Congratulations! You've created a shuttle project! We're officially done here!

In all seriousness though, now you should see three new files: project, shuttle.json and src/main.bash.

Directory tree of a new shuttle project
.
├── project
├── shuttle.json
└── src
    └── main.bash

Note! All shuttle script source files must always end in .bash

The project file is your projects 'front' entry point, and it's where you call your script. The entry point of the literal code is inside the src/main.bash file. The function main doesn't need to exist, it's just the template. You are free to format your code however you like.

Only add code to the project file if you're looking to start your code via a custom entry environment. If you don't know, don't modify it.

items.title: shuttle.json
items.text:
shuttle.json is the project settings file. It is always called this. The default values are provided here for convenience. It intentionally isn't needed, though it allows shuttle to better understand and properly handle your project.

'shuttle.json' default values
{
    "id": "user.project",
    "name": "project",
    "version": "0.1",
    "type": "script"
}

items.title: Running the project
items.text:
You can run the project also, though there is one caveat. You must always run uncompiled shuttle script source code from the root directory of the project. This is because of how the source command resolves file location.

As mentioned above, just run the project file (the 'front' entry point) from your projects root. Remember, the file name is based on your project's name.

Run a shuttle project called 'project'
./project

It really isn't that hard folks, it's just glorified scripting.

items.title: Building the project
items.text:
Building a project with shuttle is easy.

Build a project in the current directory
shuttle build

This builds the project that is inside the current directory. If you weren't inside a project directory, shuttle would error.

If you want to build a project that's in a different directory, you can specify the directory after build:

Build a project in the directory 'project'
shuttle build project

Simple enough, right? Like stated (and demonstrated), it's just glorified scripting.

The project build output location is inside the root directory of your project under the name project.bash.

items.title: Sourcing files
items.text: Sourcing different files inside a codebase is the entire point of shuttle. It's how shuttle is able to be useful at all.

items.title: What is sourcing?
items.text:
If you don't know, the source command is a shell-builtin that allows you to run commands from another file, and keep the changes made to your shell. Shuttle uses it to split the code between multiple files.

View the 'source' commands help page inside bash
help source

items.title: Sourcing a project file
items.text:
You can source a project file with two simple rules.

  • The sourced file passed to source must always start with ./ and end in .bash
  • The sourced file path must start from the project root

The cool thing about shuttle is that all file references starting with ./ and ending with .bash will be converted to their function counterparts when building. This allows you to both source a full path1 (hard-linked) and a relative or partial path (soft-linked) to a file.

Hard-linked examplePartially soft-linked exampleFully soft-linked example

This will resolve to ./src/another_file.bash in source and src_another_file when compiled.

main() {
    echo "hi I'm code"
    source ./src/another_file.bash
}

main

This will resolve to ./src/another_file.bash in source and src_another_file when compiled.

main() {
    echo "hi I'm code"

    relative_path="another_file"

    echo "hi I'm more code"

    source ./src/$relative_path.bash
}

main

This will resolve to ./src/another_file.bash in source and src_another_file when compiled.

main() {
    echo "hi I'm code"

    relative_path="./src/another_file.bash"

    echo "hi I'm more code"

    source $relative_path
}

main

All of these are fully valid in shuttle, thanks to some clever regex.

items.title: Debugging
items.text:
Be sure to report bugs to the issues page on GitHub!

Not every single situation will work, we understand that. Luckily, we thought of this before it happened. We've created an incredibly verbose 'verbose' mode in shuttle's build command for the purpose of debugging and analysis. Every source conversion is logged when this mode is turned on, allowing you to see and change the necessary things to get it working again.

shuttle's build command with the verbose flag
shuttle build --verbose
# shortened: shuttle b -v

Beware though, this is stupidly verbose.

  1. As long as it starts from the project root with a ./ ↩

items.title: Special Folders
items.text:
Shuttle's special folders are both to simplify the build system whilst also providing organization to the project.

Shuttle currently has one special folder.

items.title: lib/texts
items.text:
In a simple summary, the lib/texts/ directory is where all of the multi-line text goes.

This directory was created because the build system would be too slow and advanced if it had to take here-docs and other multi-line quirks into account. To simplify this, this directory was established as the "no edit" directory.

Any and all files inside this directory will not be modified when building shuttle.

Remember: files in this directory still have to end in .bash

Directory tree of the lib/texts directory with a 'hello_world.bash' file
.
├── lib
│   └── texts
│       └── hello_world.bash
├── project
└── src
    └── main.bash

items.title: Getting Started
items.text:
If you are new to shuttle, or if you're trying to install in general, read the installation page.

If you're looking to develop with shuttle, see the page on developing with shuttle.

Warning

Shuttle is not responsible for any damage to your projects or your computer. While we review each project in the Shuttle Script Library, it is ultimately your job to review and ensure validity of each project.

items.title: Distros
items.text: Because Shuttle is a shell script, it should run the exact same on every distro unless your shell is modified, which it isn't. However, it is important to note that shuttle requires other tools that might not be present on your system, and you have to install them yourself.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
Shuttle requires the following to be present on your system and inside $PATH in order to function as intended.

  • ripgrep (rg)
  • jq language tool (jq)
  • curl (curl)
  • git CLI (git)

You can install these yourself with your package manager.

items.title: Downloading Shuttle
items.text:
Shuttle is only available officially through the GitHub repository.

git clone https://github.com/eiedouno/shuttle
cd shuttle

items.title: Installing Shuttle
items.text:
Shuttle is a shell script, which doesn't need to be compiled. As such, you can run shuttle both compiled1 and from source.

To capitalize on this feature, you can use shuttle's source code to build a compiled version of itself and install it.

To install use the install command:

./shuttle install

After that's finished with no errors, you can delete the downloaded source code.

cd ..
rm -rf shuttle

items.title: Uninstalling
items.text:
Shuttle is intentionally easy to uninstall. If you've already deleted the source code, all you have to do is use shuttle's uninstall feature.

shuttle uninstall shuttle

items.title: All modified directories
items.text:
All of the directories shuttle touches are kept here for full cleanup if desired.

$HOME/.cache/shuttle (downloaded projects) $HOME/.config/shuttle (config) $HOME/.local/bin (installed shuttle projects) /usr/local/bin (computer-wide installed shuttle projects)

  1. "Compiled" in shuttle's terms refers to a shuttle project that has been compiled into one file using shuttle's "build" feature. ↩

items.title: Using Shuttle
items.text: This guide assumes you already have shuttle installed. If you don't, see installing.

items.title: Installing Projects
items.text:
Warning

Shuttle is not responsible for any damage to your projects or your computer. While we review each project in the Shuttle Script Library, it is ultimately your job to review and ensure validity of each project.

Shuttle is a package manager which installs projects from their upstream git repositories. So logically, the project must have a git repo for it to be downloadable by shuttle.

To install a project, simply type shuttle install followed by either the project's repository URL or the ID of the project inside the SSL1.

Examples:

shuttle install project

shuttle install https://github.com/user/project

items.title: Uninstalling Projects
items.text:
Shuttle isn't limited to only shuttle projects!

Shuttle isn't limited to uninstalling only shuttle projects, it deletes files from directories. As such, any file that is inside $HOME/.local/bin/ as a user and /usr/local/bin/ as root are able to be deleted by shuttle.

Why?

Our reason for doing this is because we didn't want shuttle to have a database file which tracks all of it's installed projects. It would make shuttle more bloated as well as make many different possible edge-cases. The trade off is allowing shuttle to delete files in the directories they're install in. To mitigate this risk, we ask the user before deleting, overrideable with --force.

Uninstalling projects is just as easy. Simply type shuttle uninstall followed by the name of the project.

Examples:

shuttle uninstall project

  1. The Shuttle Script Library is a list of projects and their URLs built into shuttle. ↩
